segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Neil.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: And I'm Pippa. When it comes to household chores, jobs like cleaning, washing clothes

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: or looking after the kids, it's often women who do most of the work. Here, two female listeners

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: of BBC World Service programme People Fixing the World share their experiences. Do they

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: sound familiar to you? I do everything. I do all the house chores. I do the food shopping. I do all

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: the cooking. I clean the bathroom. Are the chores done equally between me and my husband? No, they're

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: not done equally. I do most of the chores. So you're a family man, Neil. Do you do your fair

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: share of household chores?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I think so. My wife works part-time and I work full-time. So when I'm

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: not working, I do things and when she's not working, she does things.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Yeah, it's similar in my house. So me and my husband try to split things. But it's difficult,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: isn't it?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: It is.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Of course, no one enjoys cleaning the toilet or taking out the bins. But there is a serious

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: side to the issue. Figures from UN Women, an organisation promoting gender equality,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: suggest that every day women around the world spend three hours more than men on unpaid care

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: and domestic work So in this episode we be hearing about two projects helping husbands and wives share the housework more fairly

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And as usual you find a quiz and a worksheet to go with this episode on our website bbclearningenglish

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But now I have a question for you, Pippa.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: According to a survey conducted by Good Housekeeping magazine earlier this year, what is the most hated household chore in Britain?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Is it a. deep cleaning the oven?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: B. Scrubbing the toilet

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: or C. Cleaning the windows?

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: I'm going to say deep cleaning the oven

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: because I really hate that job.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: I hardly ever do it.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I don't like any of those

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: but we'll find out the answer

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: at the end of the programme.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Now, the first project we're going to look at

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: is on the remote Indonesian island of Rote.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Here, men traditionally work as rice farmers

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: or fishermen while women look after the home,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: the children and older people.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But with few washing machines and no running water,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: these domestic chores take a long time.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: The NGO Arunji runs a project trying to change attitudes

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: about the role of the island's women.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: They work alongside community leaders like Mama Shilpa,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: who spoke with BBC World Service reporter Ade Mardiyati.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: It is expected that the tasks done in the house,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: like holding the child, feeding the child,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: washing dishes, cooking,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: will all be done by the mother.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Silpa tells me these are all considered women work And you might be thinking well the man is busy in the fields so it just a fair division of labour But Silpa tells me women also help out in the fields

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: On Rote, cleaning, cooking and sweeping are considered women's work,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: a negative term for boring and repetitive tasks which are traditionally done by women.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Many cultures have a division of labour, a way of organising work where different tasks are done by different groups of people.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: but on Roete, this means women work even harder,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: helping out with the farming and fishing too.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: You might think this only happens in traditional societies,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: but research suggests that women in wealthy countries

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: also spend much more time on unpaid care work than men.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: One such country is Croatia,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: where the NGO Status M run their Super Dads project.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Project worker Ana Maria Socho leads workshops

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: encouraging dads and sons to take some of the pressure off mums.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Here, she explains the benefits of this to the BBC World Service.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Mothers have, you know, of course, more space for their careers, for hobbies,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: or just simply to rest, I mean, just to take a breather.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Women tend to especially appreciate men who do these kinds of chores.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And when they start pulling their weight,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: and they jokingly say that, yeah, women tend to neck less.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Sometimes mums need to take a breather,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: an informal way of saying stop and rest a while

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Anna Maria also thinks women appreciate it when their husbands pull their weight If you pull your weight you work as hard as everyone else

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Both these NGO projects agree about one thing

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Men doing more to help around the house results in happier homes, even if that means cleaning the

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: toilet now and then. And speaking of cleaning the toilet, what was the answer to your quiz question,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Neil?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I asked you what chore is the most hated in Britain.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: I thought it was cleaning the

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: oven.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, I'm afraid that's not the right answer. People hate cleaning the windows even

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: more than scrubbing the oven. Apparently 23% of the people who did the survey said cleaning

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: the windows. OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learnt starting with chores household

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: tasks like cleaning, washing and ironing that have to be done regularly.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: If you do your fair share of work, you do a reasonable amount.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Women's work is a negative term for the boring and repetitive tasks which are stereotypically done by women.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: The division of labour is a way of organising work where different tasks are done by different groups of people.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: The idiom take a breather means to stop what you're doing for a short time and rest.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: And finally, if you pull your weight, you work as hard as everyone else doing the same job.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: But remember, you can find a free transcript,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: including all the vocabulary, on our website at bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Goodbye for now.

segments.speaker: Neil
